title: A hymn in Vadhans
hook: a wedding song about a horse and a lament that begins with praise, a few pages apart

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Vadhans, peacocks in the rain, and your line was joy and grief. When someone shared news, could you let them have the whole of it? Day one thousand eighty-one.

What's the first word of a funeral song? In Guru Nanak's laments in Raga Vadhans, it's blessed. A few pages earlier in the same raga, the music is for a different scene: a horse groomed and saddled in a lane strung with lights, relatives singing, the groom climbing on, the drum starting up. Yesterday we saw that Vadhans holds wedding songs and songs of mourning. Today we open one of each. Today: a hymn in Vadhans.
screen: `A LAMENT THAT BEGINS: BLESSED.` → `A HORSE IN A LANE OF LIGHTS.` → `ONE RAGA, BOTH SONGS.`

segments.voice: First, the wedding. Guru Ram Das's ghorian, the songs of the wedding horse, start with a surprise of their own. The horse isn't a horse. In plain English: this body is the mare, and the Lord made it. Blessed is the human body, the song says, gained by good fortune. Then it puts on the saddle of understanding what is good, and rides the mare across the hard road toward the Lord. The groom's ride to the bride's home becomes the soul's ride toward God. Anyone who has seen a groom set out has the picture already; the Guru only changes who's riding where. Now the lament. Guru Nanak's alahnian open, in plain English: blessed is the Creator, the true King, who has set the whole world to its tasks. A mourning song that starts by praising the One who made the order the death belongs to. Later the alahnian say it plainly: whoever comes must rise and go. That's not cold comfort. It sets the grief inside the Creator's order instead of outside it, so the mourners aren't left alone with it. Put the two side by side. Both are about leaving. A groom leaves to begin a household; a soul leaves this world. Both are about a journey toward the Lord. And both are sung in Vadhans. The Gurus didn't need one sound for celebration and another for loss. The same music walks with a family through both doors. Today's line: the same raga for both.
screen: `GHORIAN: THE BODY IS THE MARE.` · `RIDING TOWARD THE LORD.` · `ALAHNIAN: BLESSED IS THE CREATOR.` · `WHOEVER COMES MUST GO.` · then, large: `THE SAME RAGA FOR BOTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one breath for a beginning, one for an ending. Sit, and settle. With the next in-breath, think of a beginning you've witnessed, a wedding, a birth, a first day. With the out-breath, think of an ending, a goodbye, a funeral, a last visit. Keep going, in for beginnings, out for endings, letting them come and go in the same rhythm. Notice it's one breath doing both. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the turn of each breath. If you don't, let the rhythm carry you. Later, listen to one Vadhans shabad, a ghori or an alahni. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Vadhans. Guru Ram Das's wedding-horse song, where the body is the mare, and Guru Nanak's lament, which opens by blessing the Creator. Today's word.
Your line: the same raga for both. Today, notice one beginning and one ending in your own day, a first cup, a last meeting, and greet both the same way. Day one thousand eighty-one.

howItsDone: Guru Ram Das's ghorian and Guru Nanak's alahnian are both sung in Raga Vadhans; the ghorian are associated with weddings and the alahnian with mourning, and both turn the occasion toward remembrance of God.

original.note: ghorian, songs of the wedding horse; in Guru Ram Das's, the body is the mare.

trapdoor: what you thought: one raga for weddings and funerals sounds like a mix-up.
what it means: both songs are about leaving and a journey toward the Lord, so one music carries both.
what a scholar hears: Guru Ram Das reshapes the folk ghorian into the soul's ride to God, and Guru Nanak's alahnian, a lament form, open with praise of the Creator.

notes: Ghorian (M4, Ang 575) paraphrased: the body is the mare the Lord created; blessed is the human body, gained by good fortune; saddled with the Guru's word, ridden toward the Lord. Please confirm the paraphrase and Ang.

Alahnian (M1) paraphrased: opening 'dhan sirandha sacha patisahu jin jag dhandhai laia' (blessed is the Creator, the true King, who set the world to its tasks) and 'baba aaia hai uth chalna' (whoever comes must rise and go). Please confirm Angs and that 'blessed' is a fair rendering of the opening word.
The hook's wedding and mourning scenes are illustrations, not claims about when these shabads are sung. howItsDone says 'associated with'; please confirm.
Original: ਘੋੜੀਆ, GHO-ree-aan; please confirm spelling as it appears in the Granth's heading.

Editor pass: three scene-fragment hook openings ran in a row (1079–1081), so the hook now opens on a question about the lament's first word. 'Saddles the mare with the Guru's word' changed to follow the text (deh paavau jeen bujh changa: the saddle of understanding the good; crossing the hard road), in voice and myth. The carry no longer asks the listener to call or write to someone, which repeated days 1068–1069.
